questions.question: What does the integral test link?
options: Convergence of a series and of a related improper integral.
The derivative of a function and its maximum
The value of an integral and the exact sum of every series.
The domain of a function and its codomain
questions.explanation: The integral test links convergence of $\sum f(n)$ to convergence of $\int_1^\infty f(x)dx$.

The test does not give every exact sum.
Domain and codomain are not compared.

questions.question: A student applies the integral test and then reports the exact value of $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty}f(n)$ from the integral comparison alone. What is the issue?

The integral must always equal the sum
Convergence information, not the exact value of the sum.
The function must take only integer values
questions.explanation: The integral test decides convergence (the series and integral converge or diverge together), but does not give the sum's value; the integral and series generally have different values.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted; Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: The integral test does concern infinite series; its subject is precisely the convergence of $\sum f(n)$, so this denial is wrong.

The integral need not equal the sum; the test compares convergence behaviour, and the two quantities generally differ, e.g. $\int_1^\infty 1/x^2\,\mathrm{d}x=1$ is not the value of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty 1/n^2$.
The function need not take integer values; it is defined on $[1,\infty)$ as a real-valued function, e.g. $f(x)=1/x^2$ takes non-integer values.
